title: From where to what: building the differential
description: How the time course turns a localization into a short list of causes, using the mechanism categories, the where-by-when grid and the child's own clock of static, progressive, regressive and episodic change, with functional disorder diagnosed from positive signs like everything else.
why: An examination can tell you where the trouble is, but it takes the time course to turn that address into a short list of causes.
objectives: Explain why the examination localizes and the history's time course suggests the cause, and when the history also matters for localization.
Use the mechanism categories and a level-by-tempo grid to turn a localization into a short, ranked differential.
Read a child's history against development: static, progressive, regressive or episodic, and age of onset as a filter.
Make functional neurological disorder a positive diagnosis from bedside signs, and know their limits.

sections.title: Why the time course matters
sections.content:
Every module so far has been about the first word in Where Before What. This one turns to the second, and to the word that connects them, which is **when**.

Brazis divides the labor between history and examination plainly. For working out where a lesion sits, the examination matters far more than the history, and the history, by which he means the way the deficits evolved over time, is what defines the cause (Brazis 2011, p. 4). His example is a hemiparesis on one side of the body. One that arrived within minutes suggests a vascular event or a seizure, one that developed over a few days suggests infection or demyelination, and one that crept up over months suggests a tumor or a degenerative process. The address is identical in all three, and only the clock separates the three differentials.

**Two coordinates**

It helps to think of the two as coordinates, with the examination telling you which structure is failing and the history telling you how it is failing. A cord lesion that appeared over minutes is a different disease from one that appeared over hours, weeks or years, and no examination could tell those four apart. The history does no better on its own, because "getting worse over weeks" means little until you know whether the weeks are passing in the cerebellum or in the muscle.

**When the history also localizes**

Brazis adds a refinement that is easy to skip. What you find on examination is the sum of everything that has happened to the patient, and sometimes that sum includes lesions laid down at different times. A third-nerve palsy and a hemiparesis on opposite sides would put a single lesion in the midbrain, but only if the two began together. If one dates from childhood and the other is new, they are two lesions, and a scan aimed at the midbrain would miss the second (Brazis 2011, p. 4). In children the birth history, the early milestones and old family photographs do the same work, and they may show that a "new" weakness has been there since infancy.

**Why localization comes first**

If you fix on the tempo before you have localized, it is easy to close the case too early, settling on "sudden, so stroke" before checking whether the findings even fit the brain. Localizing first guards against that, because once you have an address, the clock is choosing among the causes that can actually occur there rather than among every cause you can think of.
keyPoints: The examination localizes the lesion, and the time course in the history points to its cause (Brazis 2011, p. 4).

A deficit that arrives in minutes suggests a vascular event or seizure, one that develops over days suggests infection or demyelination, and one that builds over months suggests tumor or degeneration (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
The history also helps localize when findings began at different times, because two signs that look like one lesion may be two lesions laid down years apart.
Localizing before applying the tempo keeps you from fitting the findings to a diagnosis chosen too early.

question.question: A 15-year-old has a left hemiparesis. On the same examination you notice mild weakness of the right side of the face, and old photographs show it has been there since infancy. How should this change your localization?
options: Place a single lesion in the right pons, because the face and the limbs are affected on opposite sides
Set the facial weakness aside, because it is old
Treat them as two lesions of different ages, with the facial weakness an old finding and the new hemiparesis localized on its own merits
Assume a functional disorder, because the signs do not fit a single lesion
question.explanation: A crossed pattern places one lesion in the brainstem only when the signs appeared together. Here the facial weakness predates the hemiparesis by years, so the history splits them into two problems, and the new hemiparesis has to be localized in its own right. Forcing both into one pontine lesion would send the imaging to the wrong place. Setting the old finding aside throws away information that may still matter, such as a congenital cranial nerve problem, and signs that come from two lesions of different ages are no evidence of a functional disorder.

sections.title: The mechanism list
sections.content:
Once you have an address and a clock, you need a list of the ways nervous tissue can fail. Most clinicians carry some version of it, and there is nothing mysterious about the categories. What makes the list useful is that it is complete enough for nothing important to be forgotten, and that each category comes attached to the tempo and pattern it usually shows.

- **Vascular:** sudden, maximal at onset, respecting an arterial territory.
- **Seizure and migraine:** sudden or episodic, with recovery between events.
- **Infection:** hours to days, often with fever and a sick child.
- **Inflammatory and demyelinating:** days to weeks, often after an infection, sometimes multifocal.
- **Toxic and metabolic:** hours to days, usually symmetric and diffuse, often fluctuating.
- **Neoplastic:** weeks to months, steadily progressive, a growing address.
- **Degenerative, genetic and metabolic:** months to years, often symmetric and respecting a system.
- **Congenital and developmental:** present from early life, static.
- **Traumatic:** sudden, with a history that usually announces itself.
- **Functional:** variable, with positive signs of inconsistency (see section 6).

**Discrete lesions and systems**

Brazis adds a second way of dividing the list, which asks whether a disease makes **discrete lesions** or attacks a **system** (Brazis 2011, pp. 4-5). Vascular events, demyelinating plaques, infections, injuries and tumors tend to cause discrete lesions, single or multiple, whose signs meet at a point. Degenerative disorders take whole arrays of neurons that share a function instead, so their signs respect a system rather than a place. A symmetric, length-dependent pattern, in which the longest nerves fail first, is the signature of a system process and almost never of a discrete lesion.

**The pediatric additions**

Adult lists often treat the congenital and genetic categories as rare, but in child neurology they make up much of the daily work, from malformations and perinatal injury to inborn errors of metabolism, the muscular dystrophies and the hereditary neuropathies. A child's list is therefore weighted differently from an adult's, and the categories an adult neurologist would reach for last often sit near the middle of it.
keyPoints: Keep a complete list of mechanisms, with each category attached to its usual tempo and pattern.

Diseases that make discrete lesions (vascular, demyelinating, infectious, traumatic, neoplastic) give signs that meet at a point, while system diseases give signs that respect a function (Brazis 2011, pp. 4-5).
A symmetric, length-dependent pattern points to a system process rather than a discrete lesion.
In children, congenital, developmental and genetic-metabolic causes move from the margin of the list toward its center.

question.question: A 10-year-old has had slowly worsening, symmetric weakness and numbness of the feet for two years, now reaching the lower shins, with absent ankle reflexes. Which kind of mechanism does the pattern favor?
options: A discrete vascular lesion, because it involves the legs
A system process such as an inherited neuropathy, because the pattern is symmetric, length-dependent and slowly progressive
A tumor of the spinal cord, because both legs are involved
An infection, because it has lasted two years
question.explanation: A symmetric distal pattern that climbs from the toes, with lost ankle reflexes, is length-dependent, meaning the longest nerves fail first. That is the pattern of a system process rather than a discrete lesion, and two years of slow progression in a child points toward an inherited neuropathy. A vascular lesion would be sudden and would follow an arterial territory rather than a length gradient. A cord tumor would bring a sensory level and upper motor neuron signs, whereas this child has absent ankle jerks and glove-and-stocking numbness. Infection does not usually smoulder symmetrically for two years in a well child.

sections.title: Which map does the deficit obey?
sections.content:
Localization gives you an address, and the **shape** of the deficit at that address can hint at the mechanism as well, because each mechanism damages tissue along its own map. A clot follows the plumbing, a failing axon gives out along its length, and a bulging disc presses on a single segment. Asking which map a deficit obeys takes you a good part of the way from where to what.

**Seven maps**

- **Arterial territory.** Strokes respect the blood supply, so the middle cerebral artery takes the face and arm and the anterior cerebral artery takes the leg (Pearl 2014, p. 7). An arterial map that arrived in minutes says vascular.
- **Length of the axon.** In many polyneuropathies the most distal parts of the nerve fail first, and the hands are not usually involved until the legs are affected up to the knees (Pearl 2014, p. 76). A length map means the whole nerve is failing from within, from a nutritional, metabolic, toxic or inherited cause rather than a discrete lesion.
- **One root segment.** Pain, sensory change, weakness and a lost reflex that all belong to one segment mark a root (Pearl 2014, pp. 75, 78).
- **One nerve territory.** A mononeuropathy follows its nerve, whether the cause is compression, trauma or an underlying systemic disease (Pearl 2014, pp. 75, 83).
- **A level on the cord.** Loss below a line on the trunk, together with the bladder, belongs to the cord, with trauma, transverse myelitis and tumor among the causes (Pearl 2014, pp. 66-68).
- **A system of tracts.** Some diseases choose tracts rather than places. Vitamin B12 deficiency takes the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts together (Pearl 2014, pp. 73-74), and Friedreich ataxia takes the spinocerebellar tracts, corticospinal tracts and posterior columns (Pearl 2014, p. 64).
- **No map.** Tumors ignore vascular boundaries, grow between pathways and produce deficits that progress (Pearl 2014, p. 10). A deficit that crosses borders as it grows, or several lesions at once, obeys no single map.

**Using the figure**

Try sorting the eight children in the figure above before you read the feedback. Two of them land on the same map for different reasons, which is a reminder that a map can narrow the mechanism a long way and still stop short of naming the disease.

**Reading the map with the clock**

The previous section divided diseases into discrete lesions and systems (Brazis 2011, pp. 4-5), and the maps are the same idea at a finer grain. They work best when paired with tempo. A deficit on an arterial map that arrived in minutes is treated as a stroke from the start, while one on a length map that crept up over two years is not a stroke at all. The cases worth pausing over are those where map and clock disagree, and a deficit that looks territorial but has grown over weeks should make you suspect a mass that is only borrowing a territory's shape.
keyPoints: Each mechanism damages tissue along its own map, so the shape of a deficit hints at its cause.
Strokes follow arteries (Pearl 2014, p. 7), and axonal polyneuropathies follow length, reaching the hands only once the legs are involved to the knees (Pearl 2014, p. 76).
Roots follow a segment, single nerves their own territory, and the cord a level (Pearl 2014, pp. 66-68, 75-83).
Deficiency and degeneration follow systems of tracts, as in B12 deficiency and Friedreich ataxia (Pearl 2014, pp. 64, 73-74), while tumors follow no map (Pearl 2014, p. 10).
Read the map together with the clock, because a territorial deficit that grows over weeks suggests a mass rather than a stroke.

question.question: A 15-year-old has had numb, tingling feet for a year. The numbness now reaches just below both knees, and in the last month his fingertips have begun to tingle. Both ankle jerks are absent; the knee jerks are present; there is no sensory level on the trunk and the bladder is normal. His parents ask for an MRI of the spine to look for a tumor. Which map does the deficit obey, and what does that imply?
options: A level on the cord, so the spine MRI is the right test
One root segment on each side, so imaging of the lumbar roots is needed
No map, because both hands and feet are involved, so a mass is likely
The length of the axon, which points to a polyneuropathy from a system cause such as a toxic, nutritional or genetic one, to be pursued with nerve studies and a search for that cause
question.explanation: Symmetric loss that climbs the legs, absent ankle jerks, and fingertips that begin to tingle only once the legs are involved to about the knees make up the length map of a polyneuropathy (Pearl 2014, p. 76). That points to a system process rather than a discrete lesion, so the tests should look at the nerves and at the cause. A cord level is the tempting reading, because the parents fear a tumor, but a cord lesion gives a line on the trunk, often involves the bladder, and makes the reflexes below it brisk rather than absent (Pearl 2014, pp. 66-67). A root lesion follows one segment on one side. A mass obeys no map, whereas this deficit obeys one very precisely.

sections.title: Where × when
sections.content:
The figure above is a grid with levels down one side and tempos across the top. Choose a level and a tempo and it shows the mechanisms that fit, with pediatric examples for that address. Its purpose is modest. Once you have committed to a where and a when, the grid makes sure that the obvious candidates and the dangerous ones both reach your list, and the diagnosis is still yours to make.

**How to read it**

The cerebellum is a good place to start. **Acute** ataxia in a young child, developing over hours to a day or two, brings post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia and a toxic ingestion to the top. Stretch the same address over **weeks** and a posterior fossa tumor moves up, alongside opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia, which should send you looking for a neuroblastoma. Stretch it over **years** and inherited ataxias such as Friedreich ataxia and ataxia-telangiectasia appear. The examination of a wobbly child is the same in all three columns and only the clock changes, yet that is enough to move you from "reassure and observe" to "image the posterior fossa" to "genetic testing".

The cord works the same way. **Sudden** weakness below a level suggests trauma or an infarct. If it develops **acutely**, over hours to days, the candidates are transverse myelitis and compression from an epidural abscess or hematoma, and compression must be excluded first because decompression can treat it. A **chronic** course brings a syrinx, a tethered cord or hereditary spastic paraplegia, and a **static** picture present from birth suggests a myelomeningocele.

**Two rules the grid cannot apply for you**

The examples in each cell are illustrative. A cell can hold a rare disease that the grid does not name, and a child can have a common disease that presents at an uncommon tempo. The order of your list also depends on more than likelihood. A short list should be ranked both by how likely each diagnosis is **and** by the cost of missing it, which is why a treatable emergency such as cord compression or herpes encephalitis is acted on even when it is not yet the most probable answer.

The grid is also useful in reverse. When a disease you suspect sits in a cell that does not fit your localization or your clock, that mismatch is a reason to doubt the diagnosis, or else the localization.
keyPoints: A level-by-tempo grid turns one localization into several different differentials, separated only by time.
The same cerebellar examination suggests post-infectious ataxia or an ingestion over a day, a tumor or opsoclonus-myoclonus over weeks, and an inherited ataxia over years.
Rank the short list by likelihood and by the cost of missing a treatable emergency.
A suspected disease whose cell does not match your where or your when is a reason to doubt one of them.

question.question: A 4-year-old has become progressively unsteady over five weeks, with morning vomiting. The examination shows truncal ataxia and nothing else. Using where and when, what is the most important next step?
options: Reassure the family that post-infectious ataxia resolves on its own
Send a toxicology screen and wait
Arrange urgent brain imaging, because a cerebellar process evolving over weeks with morning vomiting places a posterior fossa tumor at the top of the list
Order nerve conduction studies to look for a neuropathy
question.explanation: The ataxia is truncal, which places the problem in the midline cerebellum, and it has developed over weeks rather than a day or two, with morning vomiting that suggests raised pressure. A cerebellar address with a subacute tempo puts a posterior fossa tumor at the top of the list, and imaging is the step that answers the question. Post-infectious ataxia is an acute illness that improves rather than worsens over the following weeks. A toxicology screen suits an acute ataxia better than a steadily progressive one, and nerve studies look at the peripheral nervous system, which does not explain isolated truncal ataxia with vomiting.

sections.title: The child's clock
sections.content:
An adult's history is usually read against two questions, how fast the problem came on and whether it is getting worse. In a child there is a third factor, development itself, and it changes the meaning of the other two.

**Four tempos that belong to childhood**

- **Static:** present from early life and not worsening. Cerebral palsy is the model, defined as a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture attributed to non-progressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain ([Rosenbaum 2007](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17370477/)). The lesion stays fixed while the child goes on developing around it.
- **Progressive:** the deficit itself is worsening.
- **Regressive:** skills that were present are lost. Regression is never cerebral palsy, and it moves the differential toward neurodegenerative and genetic-metabolic disease, epileptic encephalopathy and acquired encephalitis.
- **Episodic:** attacks with recovery between them, which points to seizures, migraine, channelopathies, syncope and intermittent metabolic decompensation.

**Not every episode is a lesion**

Some of the commonest episodes of childhood have no address at all. Breath-holding spells, seen from 6 months to 6 years, follow a fit of crying or a fright and are outgrown, and night terrors, which begin between 2 and 10 years, are a partial arousal from deep sleep (Pearl 2014, p. 104). The where-by-when figure lists them, along with syncope, as mimics under the episodic tempo. When the story makes them recognizable, the hunt for a lesion can stop before it starts.

**A static lesion can look progressive**

What makes this hard is that a fixed lesion unfolds as the brain matures. A child with spastic cerebral palsy may present as a floppy infant before the spasticity develops (DeMyer, p. 273). A perinatal stroke may be invisible at birth and show itself months later as early hand preference, since preferring one hand before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/home_exam.html)). The parents are seeing something new even though the lesion is old. The question that separates the two situations is whether the child is losing ground or failing to gain it, because asking whether anything is new will get a yes in both.

**Age of onset as a filter**

The age at which something first appears filters the list powerfully. A floppy newborn, a toddler who stops walking and an adolescent with a new tremor draw from different populations of disease even when the address is the same, so the where-by-when grid really becomes a three-way table of level, tempo and the age at which the clock started.

All of this serves one of the most consequential decisions in child neurology, which is recognizing the child labeled with a static condition who is in fact regressing.
keyPoints: In children, tempo includes development, so a history may be static, progressive, regressive or episodic.
Cerebral palsy is attributed to a non-progressive disturbance of the developing brain, so loss of acquired skills is never cerebral palsy (Rosenbaum 2007).
A static lesion can look new as development unfolds, as when a floppy infant later becomes spastic or a hemiparesis is revealed by hand preference before 12 months (DeMyer, p. 273; Utah).
Ask whether the child is losing ground or failing to gain it, and use the age of onset as a strong filter on the list.

question.question: A 3-year-old with a diagnosis of spastic diplegic cerebral palsy, who walked with a walker at 2, can no longer stand with support and has stopped using two-word phrases. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Reconsider the diagnosis, because loss of acquired motor and language skills is regression, which cerebral palsy by definition does not cause
Increase physiotherapy, because cerebral palsy often worsens with growth
Reassure the family that language often plateaus in cerebral palsy
Wait six months and reassess, because a static lesion can look progressive
question.explanation: Cerebral palsy is attributed to a non-progressive disturbance of the developing brain. A static lesion can unfold as the child matures, but it does not take away skills already gained, and this child has lost both standing and speech. That is regression, and it calls for re-examining the diagnosis with neurodegenerative, genetic-metabolic and epileptic causes in mind. More physiotherapy assumes a musculoskeletal problem, and although those can progress with growth, they do not take away two-word phrases. Reassuring the family, or waiting six months, mistakes losing ground for failing to gain it, and some of the causes on the regression list are treatable.

sections.title: Functional neurological disorder: a positive diagnosis
sections.content:
One more address belongs on the list, and it is the one most often reached by default. Functional neurological disorder is a disorder of how the nervous system functions rather than of its structure, and the old habit was to diagnose it only after every test had come back normal. That habit is wrong in principle and harmful in practice. Functional disorder is diagnosed the way everything else in this curriculum is diagnosed, from **positive findings** at the bedside.

**What the signs show**

A systematic review of bedside signs found 14 with controlled data, 7 motor, 5 sensory and 2 gait. Their sensitivity varied widely, from 8 to 100%, and was often low, while their specificity was consistently high, from 92 to 100% ([Daum 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23467417/)), although the evidence was only class III. The shape of those numbers tells you how to use the signs. A positive sign is strong evidence and an absent one is weak evidence, so failing to find a sign does not rule functional disorder out.

All the signs work on the same principle. Each shows either that a function said to be lost is present when the patient's attention is directed elsewhere, or that a deficit does not follow the anatomy.

- **Hoover sign and the abductor sign.** Hip extension or abduction that is weak on command returns automatically when the other leg is tested. In one study the abductor sign classified all 33 patients correctly, while Hoover sign was non-diagnostic in some patients ([Sonoo 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14707320/)).
- **Give-way weakness and co-contraction.** Full power appears for a moment and then collapses, or agonist and antagonist pull at once.
- **Sensory signs that ignore anatomy.** Loss may split exactly at the midline, vibration may differ across the two halves of one bone, or a field of vision may stay the same width at every distance (tunnel rather than funnel).
- **Gait.** Wild sways rarely end in a fall, the knees buckle without collapsing, and the walking improves with distraction.

**The limits**

Positive signs do not exclude structural disease, because patients, children among them, can have both, and the old argument between parsimony and multiplicity applies here as it does everywhere else ([Hilliard 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14762188/)). When the signs are present, the right course is to make the diagnosis, explain it as real and treatable, and keep examining.
keyPoints: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis made from bedside signs rather than a diagnosis of exclusion.
Validated positive signs have low sensitivity (8-100%) and high specificity (92-100%), so a present sign is strong evidence and an absent sign is weak (Daum 2014).
Hoover and abductor signs show automatic power returning when attention is elsewhere, and the abductor sign classified all 33 patients in its study correctly (Sonoo 2004).
Functional and structural disease can coexist, so making the diagnosis does not end the examination (Hilliard 2004).

question.question: A 14-year-old has a weak left leg. Hip extension on that side is absent on command but returns strongly when she flexes the right hip against resistance, and the left leg moves into abduction when she abducts the right. Reflexes and plantar responses are normal. Her MRI is booked for next week. What should you do now?
options: Wait for the MRI before discussing any diagnosis, because functional disorder can only be diagnosed when tests are normal
Make a positive diagnosis of functional weakness from these signs, explain it as real and treatable, and keep the planned investigations proportionate
Tell the family the weakness is not real, because power returns
Order nerve conduction studies, because the weakness may be peripheral
question.explanation: A positive Hoover sign and a positive abductor sign are specific bedside evidence of functional weakness, and with normal reflexes and plantar responses nothing suggests a structural lesion. The diagnosis can and should be made now, from the examination, and explained as a genuine, treatable disorder of how the nervous system works. Waiting for normal tests treats it as a diagnosis of exclusion, which delays treatment and implies it is whatever is left over. Telling a family the weakness is not real is both inaccurate and damaging, and nothing here points to a peripheral nerve. Any planned investigation should be proportionate, remembering that functional and structural disease can coexist.

sections.title: Reading results with a prior
sections.content:
[[m01-where-before-what|Module 1]] argued that a test result is worth what the prior makes it worth, and its figure let you watch a single false-positive rate swamp a vague question while barely denting a sharp one. This section turns that argument into something practical, which you can do with the pen before you sign the request.

**Where and when choose the test**

Localization and tempo do two jobs at once. They choose the test, so that a cord level asks for spine imaging, a length-dependent neuropathy for nerve studies and an episodic story for a recording of an event. They also set the prior, because a test aimed where the examination pointed starts with a good chance of finding the culprit. DeMyer's advice is to choose the one or two tests that best confirm or refute the tentative diagnosis rather than every test that covers every possibility, or in his phrase, "go for the jugular" (DeMyer, p. 539). Brazis warns that the "gunshot approach" to neuroimaging breeds false positives, which only careful localization avoids (Brazis 2011, p. 1).

**Every test has a background**

- **MRI.** Among more than 11 000 children aged 9 to 10 with research scans, 21.1% had an incidental finding, most needing no referral ([Li 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33749724/)).
- **EEG.** Among 382 healthy children aged 6 to 13, 6.5% had epileptiform discharges ([Borusiak 2010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20002145/)).
- **Genes.** Variants are reported on a five-tier scale whose middle tier is uncertain significance ([Richards 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25741868/)). A variant of uncertain significance in a gene that fits the localization and the clock is a lead worth following, while one in a gene that fits neither is a distraction.

None of these findings is an error, but each is common enough in well children that it needs a prior before it means anything.

**Write it down first**

Before ordering, write two lines in the notes, one giving the result you expect and the other saying what you will do with each answer. If neither a normal nor an abnormal result would change what you do, the test is not ready to be ordered, and if you cannot say what an abnormal result would mean for this child, the localization is not finished. The exercise takes a minute, and it protects the child from the finding nobody predicted and everybody then has to explain.

**When the result and the child disagree**

A result that contradicts a confident localization is not automatically the truth. Before accepting it, ask whether it is one of the background findings above, whether the test looked in the right place, and whether the examination needs repeating. The [[m12-cases|cases]] let you practice the whole sequence of where, when and what, with the test coming only at the end.
keyPoints: Localization and tempo choose the test and set its prior, so choose the one or two tests that best confirm or refute the working diagnosis (DeMyer, p. 539).
Unlocalized "gunshot" imaging breeds false positives (Brazis 2011, p. 1).
Background rates in well children include incidental MRI findings in 21.1% at 9 to 10 years (Li 2021) and epileptiform discharges in 6.5% at 6 to 13 years (Borusiak 2010).
A variant of uncertain significance is weighed against the localization and the clock rather than read as a diagnosis (Richards 2015).
Before ordering, write down the result you expect and what you will do with each answer.

question.question: A 9-year-old fainted while standing through a long assembly on a hot day: she went pale, slumped, and was herself again within a minute, with no confusion afterwards. Her examination is normal. An EEG ordered elsewhere reports a few focal epileptiform discharges. Her parents ask whether she has epilepsy. What is the best response?
options: Go back to the story, which describes a faint and set a low prior for epilepsy, and explain that discharges of this kind turn up in some healthy children, so the EEG does not by itself make the event a seizure
Start an antiseizure medicine, because the EEG shows epileptiform discharges
Order an MRI to find the source of the focal discharges before discussing the diagnosis
Repeat the EEG until a normal recording settles the question
question.explanation: The event reads as syncope, one of the common mimics of seizures (Pearl 2014, p. 104), so the prior for epilepsy was low before the EEG was done. Epileptiform discharges were found in 6.5% of healthy children aged 6 to 13 (Borusiak 2010), which means a positive EEG cannot outweigh a story that points elsewhere. Starting medication would treat the tracing rather than the child. An MRI would chase a finding the history never predicted and invite an incidental result of its own, and repeating the EEG until it comes back normal amounts to choosing the answer and then shopping for a test that agrees.

quiz.question: Two children have identical examinations: weak legs, a sensory level at the umbilicus and urinary retention. One developed it over 20 minutes during a trampoline accident, the other over two days after a cold. What does the difference tell you?
options: Nothing, because the localization is the same
That one of them must have a functional disorder
That the cause differs: trauma or infarction for the sudden onset, inflammation such as transverse myelitis or a compressing abscess for the one that evolved over days
That the sudden case needs no imaging
quiz.explanation: The examination places both lesions in the cord, and the time course chooses the cause. Onset over minutes points to an injury or a vascular event, while onset over days points to inflammation, infection or a compressing collection, so the same address with different clocks means different diseases, which is the central argument of this module. Identical examinations say nothing about which child might have a functional disorder, and a sensory level with retention is a structural pattern. Both children need urgent imaging, the sudden one to exclude a treatable compression or fracture.

quiz.question: Which statement about the history and the examination best matches Brazis's account?
options: The history localizes and the examination gives the cause
The examination localizes, and the history's time course points to the cause; the history also matters when deficits began at different times
The history is unimportant once the examination is complete
The examination is unreliable in children, so the history must do both jobs
quiz.explanation: Brazis states that the examination matters far more than the history for localizing a lesion, while the way the deficits evolved over time is what defines the cause. He adds that the history matters for localization too, because the examination can show the end result of lesions that arose at different times. Reversing the two roles gets the method backwards. The history is never unimportant, since it carries the clock, and the examination of a child is different from an adult's without being unreliable.

quiz.question: A 2-year-old's parents report she has preferred her right hand since 7 months. She has no other complaints and has never lost skills. What is the most likely tempo, and what does it imply?
options: Regressive, so a neurodegenerative disease is likely
Normal, because handedness is established by 7 months
Episodic, so an EEG is the key test
Static, because hand preference before 12 months points to weakness of the left hand from an early lesion such as a perinatal stroke
quiz.explanation: Hand preference before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand. With no loss of skills and a deficit present since infancy, the tempo is static, which fits an early fixed lesion such as a perinatal arterial stroke. Nothing has been lost, so this is not regression. Handedness does not develop until after 12 months, so a preference at 7 months is not normal, and with no history of attacks the episodic column does not apply.

quiz.question: Why do validated positive signs of functional weakness make a strong case when present but a weak case when absent?
options: Because they have high specificity but low sensitivity
Because they have high sensitivity but low specificity
Because they are only valid in adults
Because they have never been studied
quiz.explanation: In a systematic review, the validated positive signs had a specificity of 92 to 100% but a sensitivity of only 8 to 100%. High specificity means a present sign is rarely found in structural disease, which makes it strong evidence. Low sensitivity means many patients with functional disorder will not show any particular sign, so its absence proves little. The reverse pattern would make a positive sign weak evidence. The signs have been studied, although the evidence is class III, and the principle of positive diagnosis applies in children too.

quiz.question: A short differential for an acute cord syndrome lists transverse myelitis first and epidural abscess fourth, by likelihood. What should determine which is investigated first?
options: Likelihood alone, so investigate transverse myelitis first
Cost alone, so do the cheapest test first
Both likelihood and the cost of missing it, and since a compressing abscess is treatable by urgent decompression, it must be excluded at once
The family's preference
quiz.explanation: A short list is ranked by likelihood and by the consequences of missing a diagnosis. An epidural abscess compressing the cord is a surgical emergency in which delay costs function, so urgent spinal imaging to exclude it comes first even if inflammation is more probable, and the same MRI usually answers both questions. Ranking by likelihood alone risks missing the treatable emergency, and ranking by the cost of the test ignores what is at stake for the child.

quiz.question: A disease you suspect is usually chronic and progressive, but your patient's deficit appeared over hours, and your localization does not match where that disease normally lives. What should you conclude?
options: That the disease is presenting atypically, so the diagnosis stands
That the mismatch is a reason to doubt the diagnosis, the localization or the timeline, and to re-examine
That tempo is unreliable in children
That the patient has a functional disorder
quiz.explanation: Read in reverse, the where-by-when grid treats a suspected disease that sits in a cell matching neither your localization nor your tempo as a warning that something is wrong, whether in the diagnosis, the localization or the history of the time course. The right response is to re-examine the child and take the history again. Calling it an atypical presentation is sometimes correct, but that should be a conclusion reached after doubting rather than a way of protecting a favored diagnosis. Tempo is a strong clue in children, and a mismatch is no evidence of a functional disorder.

quiz.question: A 4-year-old born at 27 weeks has spastic diplegia: stiff legs, good hands, normal speech, and steady if slow progress in every skill. A gene panel sent by another team reports a variant of uncertain significance in a gene linked to a progressive white-matter disease. Her parents ask whether this changes her diagnosis. What is the best response?
options: Yes, because the variant lies in a relevant gene and the progressive disease should replace cerebral palsy as the diagnosis
Send a broader panel, because one uncertain result means the first panel was too narrow
Repeat brain imaging every six months until the variant is explained

Weigh the variant against a low prior, since the static course and the history of prematurity already fit and uncertain significance is not a diagnosis, and reopen the question if she ever begins to lose skills
quiz.explanation: Uncertain significance is the middle tier of the five-tier variant scale, neither pathogenic nor benign (Richards 2015), and its weight depends on the prior. This child's clock is static and she keeps gaining skills, and severe leg spasticity with good hands and speech is the spastic diplegia of cerebral palsy (DeMyer, p. 340), which in a child born this early already has an explanation. Rewriting the diagnosis would treat an uncertain variant as a pathogenic one. A broader panel multiplies the uncertain findings without raising the prior, and serial imaging chases the variant rather than the child. Regression is the finding that would change the prior, so it is worth naming to the family as the reason to look again.

signOff: The resident presents three new consults to a faculty reader in where, when, what form, stating the localization, the tempo and a ranked differential before any test results are known.

opener.parable: A test result behaves more like a witness than a judge. How much weight its evidence deserves depends on what you already knew when you called it, so the same report can mean a great deal in one child and very little in another.
opener.history: Thomas Bayes, an 18th-century British vicar and amateur mathematician, gave his name to the rule every clinician uses without naming it: the odds before a test, multiplied by the weight of its result, give the odds after.
